runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The first booster catch, on Flight 5 in October 2024, worked on the first attempt. The most recent one, on Flight 15, was aborted after launch, and the booster fell into the ocean instead of being caught. SpaceX's explanation for that abort has been unclear and is still under review.

sections.heading: First booster catch (Flight 5, October 2024)
points: The first Super Heavy catch happened on Flight 5 on October 13, 2024, when the booster came back to the Starbase tower and was snared by the chopstick arms on the first attempt.
It was the first time a Super Heavy booster was returned to the launch tower and caught, which made it a first for SpaceX.
The booster, B12, was not reused afterward, according to the Booster 12 record.

sections.heading: Most recent booster catch attempt (Flight 15, November 2026)
points: On Flight 15, SpaceX tried to bring the booster back to the tower for a catch, but it aborted the return a few minutes after launch.
The booster came down in the ocean instead of being caught, so the catch did not happen.
SpaceX first said a guidance issue was behind the abort, but a spokesperson later said it was not a guidance problem, and the cause was still under investigation.
Flight 15 also aimed to catch the ship upper stage with the chopsticks, which the ship did achieve.

sections.heading: How they compare
points: The first catch succeeded on the first try; the latest attempt failed, with the booster lost in the ocean.
Both used the same tower chopstick arms and the same goal of returning the booster to the launch site.
The first catch proved the concept, while the latest attempt showed that the return maneuver still carries risk even after the technique was established.

runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The first booster catch was Flight 5 in October 2024, when the launch tower caught Booster 12. The most recent successful booster catch was Flight 8 in March 2025. The newest flight, Flight 15, called off its booster catch, so the booster splashed down instead.

sections.heading: First booster catch (Flight 5, Oct 2024)
points: Flight 5 launched on October 13, 2024 with Booster 12 and Ship 30, and the tower's chopsticks caught the returning booster, the first time this had been done.
The catch came about seven minutes after liftoff, and the booster was held by the tower arms after its engines stopped.
Later reporting said the booster came within about one second of aborting the catch, according to SpaceX engineers as relayed to Elon Musk.
The booster had been caught despite damage to one of its chine sections during descent.

sections.heading: Most recent successful booster catch (Flight 8, Mar 2025)
points: Flight 8 launched on March 6, 2025 with Booster 15, and the booster returned to Starbase and was caught by the tower about seven minutes after liftoff.
The ship was lost about nine minutes into that flight, so the booster catch was the highlight rather than a full success.
Booster 15 was reflown on Flight 11 in October 2025 but was not caught; it was expended in the Gulf.
Flight 7 in January 2025 (Booster 14) was the second successful catch, sitting between the first and the Flight 8 catch.

sections.heading: Side-by-side comparison
points: Both catches used the same launch tower's chopstick arms at Starbase, and both happened roughly seven minutes after liftoff.

The first catch was a novelty demonstration; by Flight 8 the catch was a repeatable part of the test plan, with radar sensors added to the tower to improve distance measurement to the returning vehicle.
Booster 12 was an earlier prototype; Booster 15 was a Block 2 booster, so the newer catch used a later design.
Across these flights, the tower caught three boosters in total before Flight 15 (Flights 5, 7 and 8).

sections.heading: Flight 15 (most recent mission)
points: Flight 15 was the newest mission and was planned as the first attempt to catch both the booster and the ship in one flight.
The booster's catch was called off, and the booster was diverted to a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch.
Reports say the booster's systems aborted the catch because it was not where it needed to be, and the ship was later caught by the tower from orbit.
So the most recent booster catch is Flight 8, while the most recent flight's booster catch did not happen.

runs.goal: find out what the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why
runs.detail: Webb's mirror segments are beryllium, a light metal that stays stiff and keeps its shape in extreme cold. They carry a microscopically thin gold coating, which reflects infrared light much better than ordinary silver or aluminum. The gold is only a surface layer, so the mirror is not solid gold.
